question: For a Strict-Transport-Security response header received over HTTPS, through which functions does the header travel from response-header parsing to the function that allocates and stores a new HSTS entry?
build_assumptions: HTTP and HSTS enabled; HSTS turned on for the handle (data->hsts set, e.g. via CURLOPT_HSTS_CTRL); release build; header example: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains.
reference_answer:
Response headers that start with 'S' are parsed by http_header_s() in lib/http.c. It looks for 'Strict-Transport-Security:' only when the handle has an HSTS cache (data->hsts) and Curl_xfer_is_secure() is true; in a release build there is no exception for plain HTTP (only debug builds honour CURL_HSTS_HTTP). It passes the origin host name and the header value to Curl_hsts_parse(). Errors other than out-of-memory are not fatal: the function logs 'Illegal STS header skipped' and continues.

Curl_hsts_parse() in lib/hsts.c ignores IP-address hosts, because RFC 6797 excludes explicit IP addresses. It parses the directives: max-age is mandatory and is capped at two years (CAP_HSTS_MAX_AGE); a repeated max-age or includeSubDomains is an error. max-age=0 removes an existing entry that matches the host exactly and stores nothing. Otherwise the expiry becomes now plus max-age. It then looks for an existing entry with hsts_check() without subdomain matching. If one exists, it only updates that entry's expires and includeSubDomains fields; if not, it calls hsts_create().

hsts_create() is where the entry is allocated and stored. It strips a trailing dot from the host name, allocates a struct stsentry with the host name stored inline, sets expires and includeSubDomains, and calls hsts_append(). hsts_append() keeps the cache bounded: when the list already holds MAX_HSTS_ENTRIES (10000) entries, it removes and frees the first entry in the list before appending the new one at the end.

hsts_create() is also the common constructor for the other ways entries enter the cache: hsts_add_host_expire() uses it when entries are loaded from an HSTS file or the read callback, and Curl_hsts_copy() uses it when curl_easy_duphandle() copies live entries.

question: An HSTS cache created by Curl_hsts_init() can belong to a single easy handle or to a share handle (CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS). What ownership rules decide which handle frees the cache?
build_assumptions: HTTP and HSTS enabled; share support enabled; release build.
reference_answer:
Curl_hsts_init() in lib/hsts.c only allocates a struct hsts with an empty entry list. It is called from four places: CURLOPT_HSTS_CTRL with CURLHSTS_ENABLE and CURLOPT_HSTS, both when the handle has no cache yet (lib/setopt.c); curl_share_setopt() with CURLSHOPT_SHARE and CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS, which stores the cache in share->hsts (lib/curl_share.c); and curl_easy_duphandle() (lib/easy.c). There is no reference count; ownership follows from where the pointer lives.

When an easy handle is linked to a share that has an HSTS cache, Curl_share_easy_link() frees the handle's private cache with Curl_hsts_cleanup(&data->hsts) and then sets data->hsts = share->hsts. From then on every easy-side cleanup checks the condition !data->share || !data->share->hsts before freeing. Curl_close() in lib/url.c uses it. CURLOPT_HSTS_CTRL without CURLHSTS_ENABLE frees the private cache and the file list, but with a shared cache only detaches it (data->hsts = NULL). CURLOPT_HSTS set to NULL clears the file list and frees the cache only if it is not shared. Curl_close() still calls Curl_hsts_save() first, so the cache is saved even when it is shared. When the handle detaches from the share, Curl_share_easy_unlink() clears data->hsts if it points to share->hsts, without freeing it.

The share frees its own cache in two places: CURLSHOPT_UNSHARE with CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS calls Curl_hsts_cleanup(&share->hsts), and share_destroy() does the same when the share is destroyed. curl_share_setopt() refuses to change anything while the share is in use (CURLSHE_IN_USE), so an unshare cannot free a cache that easy handles still point to.

curl_easy_duphandle() never shares the pointer. It creates a new private cache, loads the configured HSTS file and read callback into it, and copies the non-expired entries from the original with Curl_hsts_copy().

CURLOPT_HSTS only records the file names in data->state.hstslist; Curl_hsts_loadfiles() loads them in Curl_pretransfer(). The comment says this is because the handle might get a shared HSTS cache to load them into.

question: When the curl tool is run with --ssl-sessions FILE, why does it import the saved TLS sessions through a fresh easy handle that has the tool's share handle attached (CURLOPT_SHARE) before calling curl_easy_ssls_import()?
build_assumptions: TLS build with session export support (USE_SSL and USE_SSLS_EXPORT, so feature_ssls_export is set in the tool); sequential (non-parallel) curl tool run.
reference_answer:
In src/tool_operate.c, operate() creates one share with curl_share_init() and configures it in share_setup(). share_setup() requests CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION among other data types (cookies, DNS, PSL, HSTS, and connections when not running in parallel). In lib/curl_share.c, curl_share_setopt() reacts to CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION by creating the share's session cache with Curl_ssl_scache_create(25, 2, ...). The --ssl-sessions option is accepted only when feature_ssls_export is set.

Before any transfer runs, operate() calls tool_ssls_load() in src/tool_ssls.c. It opens the file; a missing file only produces a note. It then calls tool_ssls_easy(), which creates an easy handle with curl_easy_init() and sets CURLOPT_SHARE to the tool's share. Each line has the form base64(shmac) ':' base64(sdata). Lines that do not parse are warned about and skipped, and each decoded pair is passed to curl_easy_ssls_import() with a NULL session key.

The reason for the share is where libcurl keeps sessions. curl_easy_ssls_import() in lib/easy.c checks its arguments (missing sdata gives CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT) and calls Curl_ssl_session_import() in lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c. That function gets the cache with cf_ssl_scache_get(), which returns the share's ssl_scache if the handle has a share with one ('its ssl_scache has preference over the multi'), else the multi handle's cache, else nothing. A fresh easy handle is in no multi, so without the share there is no cache and the import fails with CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT. With the share, the sessions land in the share's cache.

With a NULL session key, the import requires shmac_len to equal the size of the salt plus the HMAC. It then looks for a peer with a matching HMAC (cf_ssl_find_peer_by_hmac()), or takes a free peer entry, and adds the session to it.

Because the same share is later passed to run_all_transfers(), every transfer can use the imported sessions. After the transfers, tool_ssls_save() exports the sessions from the same share back to the file.

The answer must state that a fresh easy handle belongs to no multi, so without the share it would have no session cache to import into.
The answer must state that the tool's share_setup() shares CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION, which makes curl_share_setopt() create the share's session cache (Curl_ssl_scache_create).
The answer must state that the same share is used for all later transfers (run_all_transfers), so they can resume the imported sessions.
The answer must state that tool_ssls_easy() creates the easy handle with curl_easy_init() and sets CURLOPT_SHARE to the tool's share.
The answer must state that each file line is base64(shmac) ':' base64(sdata), bad lines are warned about and skipped, and a missing file is not an error.
The answer must state that with a NULL session key the import requires shmac_len equal to salt plus HMAC size and attaches the session to a peer matched by HMAC or to a free peer.

question: Why does curl_mime_free() begin by unbinding the mime handle from the part it may be attached to, before it frees any parts?
build_assumptions: MIME support enabled (CURL_DISABLE_MIME not defined).
reference_answer:
A curl_mime handle can be attached to a part as that part's content. Curl_mime_set_subparts() in lib/mime.c records the link in both directions: subparts->parent points to the part, and the part gets kind MIMEKIND_MULTIPART, arg = the mime handle, a seek function, and a free function. The free function depends on ownership. curl_mime_subparts() passes take_ownership = TRUE and installs mime_subparts_free(), so cleaning the part also frees the subparts. setopt_mimepost() in lib/setopt.c, the handler for CURLOPT_MIMEPOST, binds the application's top-level mime to the easy handle's internal part s->mimepostp with take_ownership = FALSE, which installs mime_subparts_unbind() instead. The comment of mime_subparts_unbind() says it does not free subparts but unbinds them, and that it is used for the top level only.

curl_mime_free() returns at once for NULL. Otherwise its first statement is mime_subparts_unbind(mime), with the comment 'Be sure it is not referenced anymore.' If the mime has a parent part, mime_subparts_unbind() sets the part's freefunc to NULL ('Be sure we will not be called again') and calls cleanup_part_content() on it ('Avoid dangling pointer in part'). cleanup_part_content() resets the part: arg points back to the part itself, kind becomes MIMEKIND_NONE, and the read and seek functions are cleared. Then mime->parent is set to NULL.

The reason is that the parent part would otherwise keep a pointer to memory that curl_mime_free() is about to release, together with a free function that would later act on that freed handle. For example, when an application frees a mime it had set with CURLOPT_MIMEPOST, the easy handle's internal part is reset to empty instead of keeping a dangling pointer.

After unbinding, curl_mime_free() deletes the parts without recursion. For a nested multipart part whose freefunc is mime_subparts_free, it clears the part's link to the child mime and reuses the parent pointers as a to-do chain: the child's parent field takes the current mime's parent value, and the current mime's parent field now points to the child. When the current mime has no parts left, the function frees it and continues with the next mime in that chain. Each part is cleaned with Curl_mime_cleanpart(), which frees its headers (user headers only if MIME_USERHEADERS_OWNER is set), MIME type, name and file name.

The answer must state that mime_subparts_unbind() sets the parent part's freefunc to NULL and resets its content with cleanup_part_content() to avoid a dangling pointer, then clears mime->parent.

The answer must state that a part holding subparts stores the mime handle in part->arg together with a free function (mime_subparts_free or mime_subparts_unbind), which would otherwise later act on freed memory.
The answer must state that CURLOPT_MIMEPOST binds the application's mime to the easy handle's internal part without ownership (take_ownership FALSE, mime_subparts_unbind).
The answer must state that curl_mime_subparts() attaches with ownership (mime_subparts_free), so cleaning the parent part frees the subparts.
The answer must state that cleanup_part_content() resets the part (arg back to the part, kind MIMEKIND_NONE, read/seek/free functions cleared).
The answer must state that curl_mime_free() then frees nested subparts iteratively (non-recursively), reusing the mime parent pointers as a chain of mime handles still to be freed.

question: Where do the characters of a new curl_mime handle's multipart boundary string come from?
build_assumptions: MIME support enabled; TLS build (USE_SSL); release build (no DEBUGBUILD).
reference_answer:
The boundary is created in curl_mime_init() in lib/mime.c, the public constructor of a mime handle. After allocating the handle and clearing its parent and part list, it fills mime->boundary in two steps. First, memset() writes MIME_BOUNDARY_DASHES (24) '-' characters. Second, it calls Curl_rand_alnum() to write MIME_RAND_BOUNDARY_CHARS (22) random characters directly after the dashes, starting at offset MIME_BOUNDARY_DASHES in the buffer; it passes MIME_RAND_BOUNDARY_CHARS + 1 as the size because Curl_rand_alnum() also writes the terminating NUL byte. The boundary buffer is MIME_BOUNDARY_LEN + 1 bytes, where MIME_BOUNDARY_LEN = 24 + 22 = 46. So every boundary is 24 dashes followed by 22 letters and digits. If the random generator fails, curl_mime_init() frees the new handle and returns NULL, so the caller gets no handle at all.

Curl_rand_alnum() in lib/rand.c draws each character from the 62-character alphabet 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789'. It takes one random unsigned int per character from randit() and rejects values at or above UINT_MAX - (UINT_MAX % 62), so that r % 62 has no modulo bias. The easy handle passed to curl_mime_init(easy) is forwarded to it and may be NULL.

randit() decides the source of the randomness. In a TLS build it calls Curl_ssl_random(), which asks the TLS backend through Curl_ssl->random. In a non-Windows build without TLS, weak_random() is used instead: arc4random() if available, otherwise a seeded linear congruential generator that logs 'WARNING: using weak random seed'.

The boundary is later used when the parts are prepared: mime_prepare_headers(), reached from Curl_mime_prepare_headers(), adds it to the multipart Content-Type header through add_content_type(), as '; boundary=' followed by the boundary string.

The answer must state that the random characters come from Curl_rand_alnum() in lib/rand.c, using the alphabet A-Z, a-z, 0-9.
The answer must state that Curl_rand_alnum() gets its random numbers from randit(), which in a TLS build calls Curl_ssl_random() (the TLS backend's random function).
The answer must state that Curl_rand_alnum() rejects random values at or above UINT_MAX - UINT_MAX % 62 to avoid modulo bias.
The answer must state that the size passed is MIME_RAND_BOUNDARY_CHARS + 1 because Curl_rand_alnum() also writes a terminating NUL.
The answer must state that curl_mime_init() frees the handle and returns NULL if random generation fails.
The answer must state that in a non-Windows build without TLS randit() uses weak_random() (arc4random or a seeded LCG with a warning).
